subject: biology
topicDisplay: C2–C3 — Interaction and interdependence: signalling, body systems and defence
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {subject} question that tests this idea: "{lo}". Then mark my answer the way an IB examiner would.
promptWeak: Explain this {board} {subject} idea simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake students make: "{lo}".

learningObjectives.title: A neuron is one cell with a body and long fibres
A nerve impulse is a travelling reversal of membrane potential
Synapses join neurons to neurons or to effectors, one way only
Calcium entry triggers neurotransmitter release
Parts of a living system must work together
The brain combines inputs, learns and remembers
Sensory neurons carry messages in
Motor neurons carry commands out to muscles
The pain reflex withdraws the hand before you feel it
Epinephrine readies the body for hard exercise
Heart rate is adjusted by feedback from pressure and chemical sensors
Pathogens cause infectious disease, and observation beat germ theory to it
Clotting seals a cut
Innate is broad and fixed; adaptive is specific and learns
Lymphocytes cooperate to make antibodies
HIV passes only in certain body fluids
Antibiotics hit bacterial processes, which viruses do not have
Resistance evolves by natural selection, so use antibiotics carefully
Vaccines deliver antigens, not the disease
Percentage change and percentage difference

questions.q: A motor neuron has its cell body in the spinal cord and a single fibre about 1 m long that reaches a muscle in the foot. What is this fibre?
options: One of the neuron's several axons, each of which reaches a different muscle in the leg.
An axon: a single long fibre along which impulses are conducted away from the cell body.
A nerve, because a fibre this long must be made of many neurons joined end to end.
A connecting fibre that links the neuron to the muscle but is not part of the neuron itself.
optionWhy: A student who thinks a neuron has several axons picks this. In fact a neuron has a single axon; its branches near the end are terminals of that one axon.
An axon is a long single fibre projecting from the cell body. A motor neuron's axon can extend about a metre from the spinal cord to a muscle, and impulses are conducted along it.
A student who confuses a nerve with a neuron picks this. In fact one neuron's axon can be a metre long; a nerve is a bundle of many such fibres.
A student who sees fibres as separate wiring picks this. In fact the fibre is part of the neuron: an extension of its cytoplasm surrounded by its own membrane.
questions.explain: An axon is a long single fibre projecting from the cell body. A motor neuron's axon can extend about a metre from the spinal cord to a muscle, and impulses are conducted along it.

questions.q: Why is a nerve impulse described as an electrical signal?
options: It consists of electrons flowing along the inside of the fibre, in the same way as a current in a metal wire.
It consists of positively charged ions moving across the membrane, which changes the membrane potential.
It consists of neurotransmitter molecules travelling along the fibre and carrying their electrical charge with them.
It consists of sodium ions flowing along the whole length of the fibre from one end of it to the other.
optionWhy: A student who applies the wiring analogy literally picks this. In fact no electrons flow along the axon; the charge carriers are ions crossing the membrane.

A nerve impulse is electrical because it involves movement of positively charged ions, sodium and potassium ions, across the membrane of the nerve fibre, reversing and then restoring the membrane potential.
A student who generalizes the chemical signal at synapses to the whole neuron picks this. In fact neurotransmitters act only at synapses; along the fibre the signal is a change in membrane potential.

A student who thinks the ions themselves travel the length of the axon picks this. In fact ions cross the membrane at each point in turn; the impulse travels but the individual ions move only a short distance.
questions.explain: A nerve impulse is electrical because it involves movement of positively charged ions, sodium and potassium ions, across the membrane of the nerve fibre, reversing and then restoring the membrane potential.

questions.q: Which statement about a synapse is correct?
options: A signal can pass across it in either direction, depending on which of the two neurons is stimulated first.
It is found only where two neurons meet, so muscle fibres are stimulated directly by the nerve impulse.
A signal can pass across it in one direction only, from the presynaptic cell to the postsynaptic cell.
The action potential jumps across the gap as an electrical spark, so no chemical is needed to cross the cleft.
optionWhy: A student who pictures the synapse as a simple gap picks this. In fact only one side releases neurotransmitter and only the other has receptors, so transmission is one-way.
A student who has only seen neuron-to-neuron synapses picks this. In fact synapses also occur between neurons and effector cells; a neuromuscular junction is a synapse.
A signal can only pass in one direction across a typical synapse, because neurotransmitter is released from the presynaptic membrane and its receptors are on the postsynaptic membrane.
A student who assumes electricity bridges the cleft picks this. In fact the signal crosses the cleft as a neurotransmitter that diffuses to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane.
questions.explain: A signal can only pass in one direction across a typical synapse, because neurotransmitter is released from the presynaptic membrane and its receptors are on the postsynaptic membrane.

questions.q: What is the role of calcium ions in the release of neurotransmitter from a presynaptic neuron?
options: Depolarization of the presynaptic membrane opens calcium channels; calcium ions enter and signal vesicles to fuse with the membrane.
Calcium ions are released from the presynaptic neuron and diffuse across the cleft, where they then depolarize the postsynaptic membrane.
Calcium ions have no role, because neurotransmitter simply diffuses out through the presynaptic membrane when an impulse arrives.
Calcium ions provide the energy for carrier proteins to pump the neurotransmitter across the synaptic cleft to its postsynaptic receptors.
optionWhy: When an action potential depolarizes the presynaptic membrane, calcium ions are taken up into the neuron. Inside the neuron they act as a signalling chemical that causes vesicles of neurotransmitter to fuse with the presynaptic membrane, releasing it into the cleft.
A student who confuses calcium with the neurotransmitter picks this. In fact calcium ions move into the presynaptic neuron and act inside it; the neurotransmitter is what crosses the cleft.
A student who assumes release is passive diffusion picks this. In fact neurotransmitter is stored in vesicles and released by exocytosis, which is triggered by calcium ion entry.
A student who thinks neurotransmitter is actively transported across the cleft picks this. In fact it diffuses across the cleft; calcium ions are a signal for release, not an energy source.
questions.explain: When an action potential depolarizes the presynaptic membrane, calcium ions are taken up into the neuron. Inside the neuron they act as a signalling chemical that causes vesicles of neurotransmitter to fuse with the presynaptic membrane, releasing it into the cleft.

questions.q: Which statement best describes what is meant by integration in a living system?
options: Coordination of the component parts so that together they perform an overall function that none performs alone.
Each component part performs its own function independently, so the parts do not need to interact.
A single dominant part carries out the overall function while the other parts play no role in it.
Coordination is achieved only by conscious decisions, so it applies only to organisms with a brain.
optionWhy: Integration is a necessary process in living systems: coordination is needed for the component parts of a system to collectively perform an overall function.
A student who pictures body systems as separate machines picks this. Parts that do not interact cannot perform a collective function; integration is the coordination between them.
A student who assigns each function to one 'responsible' system picks this. An overall function of a system emerges from all its parts working together, not from one part alone.
A student who equates coordination with conscious control picks this. Integration occurs at every level of living systems, including unconscious processes and organisms with no brain at all.
questions.explain: Integration is a necessary process in living systems: coordination is needed for the component parts of a system to collectively perform an overall function.

questions.q: A tennis player watches the ball, hears it hit the opponent's racket, senses the position of her own arm and remembers where the opponent usually aims. What is the role of her brain in producing her return shot?
options: It combines the information from all these inputs with stored memory and uses the result to decide the response.
It processes each input in its own region, and each region sends its own response to the muscles.
It only supplies timing, because the movement itself is stored in the arm muscles from previous practice.
It uses only the input she is consciously aware of, sight, since the brain cannot process input unconsciously.
optionWhy: The brain is the central information integration organ: it processes information combined from several inputs (sight, hearing, body position) together with learning and memory, and produces one coordinated response.

A student who pictures the brain as a set of independent sensory modules picks this. Separate responses from each sense would conflict; the brain integrates the inputs before a single motor output is sent.
A student who takes 'muscle memory' literally picks this. Learning and memory are functions of the brain; muscles store nothing and contract only when motor neurons stimulate them.
A student who thinks all brain processing is conscious picks this. Much of the brain's integration, such as using the sense of arm position, happens without awareness; all the inputs contribute.
questions.explain: The brain is the central information integration organ: it processes information combined from several inputs (sight, hearing, body position) together with learning and memory, and produces one coordinated response.

questions.q: What is the function of sensory neurons?
options: They carry impulses out from the central nervous system to the receptors that must then respond.
They detect every stimulus themselves, so the body needs no separate receptor cells.
They convey impulses from receptor cells to the spinal cord and the cerebral hemispheres.
They are the nerves that connect each sense organ to the brain, each made of one long fibre.
optionWhy: A student who has swapped the two neuron types picks this. Impulses out of the CNS travel along motor neurons to effectors; receptors do not respond, they detect. Sensory neurons carry input inwards only.

A student who generalizes from the free nerve ending of the pain reflex picks this. In most sense organs, separate receptor cells (such as photoreceptors in the retina) detect the stimulus and signal to the sensory neuron.
Sensory neurons convey messages from receptor cells to the central nervous system, providing the input to the spinal cord and cerebral hemispheres.

A student who treats nerve and neuron as the same thing picks this. A sensory neuron is a single cell; a nerve is a bundle of fibres from many neurons, usually including both sensory and motor fibres.
questions.explain: Sensory neurons convey messages from receptor cells to the central nervous system, providing the input to the spinal cord and cerebral hemispheres.

questions.q: A person decides to straighten their arm. How does output from the cerebral hemispheres produce this movement?
options: Motor neurons stimulate the triceps to contract and other motor neurons stimulate the biceps to lengthen actively.
Sensory neurons carry the command from the cerebral hemispheres down to the triceps, causing it to contract.
Epinephrine released into the blood stimulates the triceps to contract, because hormones control the skeletal muscles.
Motor neurons stimulate the triceps to contract, and the biceps relaxes because it is no longer stimulated.
optionWhy: A student who thinks a nerve can drive a muscle in both directions picks this. Muscles can only be stimulated to contract; the biceps is lengthened by the contraction of its antagonist, not by a signal to extend.
A student who has swapped the neuron types picks this. Sensory neurons carry input to the CNS; output from the cerebral hemispheres to muscles is through motor neurons.

A student who thinks epinephrine causes muscle action picks this. Skeletal muscle contracts when stimulated by motor neurons; epinephrine prepares the body for activity but does not command a movement.

Output from the cerebral hemispheres reaches muscles through motor neurons, which stimulate contraction. The triceps contracts to straighten the arm; the biceps relaxes because stimulation of it is withdrawn, and it is lengthened passively.
questions.explain: Output from the cerebral hemispheres reaches muscles through motor neurons, which stimulate contraction. The triceps contracts to straighten the arm; the biceps relaxes because stimulation of it is withdrawn, and it is lengthened passively.

questions.q: A person touches a hot pan and withdraws their hand before feeling any pain. Which sequence describes the reflex arc that produced the withdrawal?
options: free nerve ending → sensory neuron → spinal cord → cerebral hemispheres → motor neuron → skeletal muscle of the arm
free nerve ending → sensory neuron → interneuron in the spinal cord grey matter → motor neuron → smooth muscle of the arm
free nerve ending → sensory neuron → interneuron in spinal cord grey matter → motor neuron → skeletal muscle of the arm
skeletal muscle of the arm → sensory neuron → interneuron in the grey matter of the spinal cord → motor neuron → free nerve ending
optionWhy: A student who thinks the brain must decide picks this. The reflex is integrated in the spinal cord; impulses do also travel to the brain, but the withdrawal has already been triggered before they arrive.
A student who thinks involuntary responses must use involuntary muscle picks this. The effector in the pain reflex is skeletal muscle; the arm has no smooth muscle that could move it.

The pain reflex arc has a free sensory nerve ending as the receptor, a sensory neuron into the spinal cord, a single interneuron in the grey matter, a motor neuron out, and skeletal muscle as the effector.
A student who has swapped receptor and effector picks this. The free nerve ending detects the stimulus and so comes first; the muscle carries out the response and so comes last.
questions.explain: The pain reflex arc has a free sensory nerve ending as the receptor, a sensory neuron into the spinal cord, a single interneuron in the grey matter, a motor neuron out, and skeletal muscle as the effector.

questions.q: A sprinter waits for the starting signal and epinephrine is secreted into the blood. Which set of effects of epinephrine helps to facilitate intense contraction of the leg muscles during the race?
options: Faster heart rate and an equal increase in blood flow to every organ, including the gut, the skin and the kidneys.
Direct transfer of energy from the adrenal glands to the leg muscle fibres, so that they can contract more strongly.
Direct stimulation of the leg muscle fibres to contract, taking over from the motor neurons for the duration of the race.
Faster heart rate, wider bronchioles, glycogen breakdown in the liver and more blood flow to skeletal muscle.
optionWhy: A student who reasons that more output means more blood everywhere picks this. Epinephrine redistributes blood: vessels to the gut and skin constrict while those to skeletal muscle dilate.
A student who takes 'adrenaline rush' as a burst of energy picks this. Epinephrine is a signal; the energy for contraction comes from cell respiration of glucose in the muscle.
A student who thinks the hormone commands the movement picks this. Skeletal muscle contracts only when stimulated by motor neurons; epinephrine prepares the body but does not replace nervous control.

These widespread effects of epinephrine increase the delivery of oxygen and glucose to the muscles: more cardiac output, easier ventilation, higher blood glucose and blood diverted to skeletal muscle, allowing intense cell respiration and contraction.
questions.explain: These widespread effects of epinephrine increase the delivery of oxygen and glucose to the muscles: more cardiac output, easier ventilation, higher blood glucose and blood diverted to skeletal muscle, allowing intense cell respiration and contraction.

questions.q: Which statement gives the location and the function of the receptors that provide sensory input for the control of heart rate?
options: Baroreceptors and chemoreceptors are both in the wall of the heart, where they monitor the pressure and the chemistry of the blood as it passes through it.
Baroreceptors in the aorta and carotid arteries monitor blood pressure; chemoreceptors there and in the medulla monitor pH, oxygen and carbon dioxide.
Baroreceptors in the aorta monitor blood pressure and chemoreceptors in the carotid arteries monitor only the concentration of oxygen.
Baroreceptors and chemoreceptors are both located in the medulla, which monitors the pressure and chemistry of the blood flowing through it.
optionWhy: A student who expects the heart to monitor itself picks this. The receptors are in the major arteries leaving the heart and in the medulla, not in the heart wall.

Baroreceptors are stretch receptors in the walls of the aorta and carotid arteries. Chemoreceptors in the same arteries and in the medulla monitor blood pH and the concentrations of oxygen and carbon dioxide. Both send impulses to the medulla.

A student who thinks oxygen is the only chemical sensed picks this. Chemoreceptors monitor pH and carbon dioxide as well as oxygen, and they are found in the aorta and medulla as well as the carotid arteries.
A student who places all the sensors in the brain picks this. The medulla does contain chemoreceptors, but baroreceptors are in the artery walls, where stretch can be detected directly.
questions.explain: Baroreceptors are stretch receptors in the walls of the aorta and carotid arteries. Chemoreceptors in the same arteries and in the medulla monitor blood pH and the concentrations of oxygen and carbon dioxide. Both send impulses to the medulla.

questions.q: Which statement about the organisms that cause infectious diseases in humans is correct?
options: Viruses, bacteria, fungi and protists all include species that are human pathogens, but archaea are not known to be.
Archaea, like bacteria, include many species that are human pathogens, because both groups are prokaryotes.
Only bacteria and viruses cause infectious diseases in humans; fungi and protists do not cause any.
Any microorganism that lives on or inside the human body is, by definition, a pathogen and a cause of disease.
optionWhy: A disease-causing organism is a pathogen, and the term is typically reserved for viruses, bacteria, fungi and protists. Archaea, although they are prokaryotes, are not known to cause any diseases in humans.
A student who treats 'prokaryote' as meaning 'germ' picks this. Being a prokaryote does not make an organism a pathogen; archaea are not known to cause any human disease.
A student whose examples of infectious disease are all bacterial or viral picks this. Fungi and protists also include human pathogens, such as the causes of athlete's foot and malaria.
A student who equates microorganisms with 'germs' picks this. A pathogen is defined by causing disease; most microorganisms on the skin and in the gut cause none.
questions.explain: A disease-causing organism is a pathogen, and the term is typically reserved for viruses, bacteria, fungi and protists. Archaea, although they are prokaryotes, are not known to cause any diseases in humans.

questions.q: Which sequence correctly describes the events that seal a cut in the skin?
options: Platelets release clotting factors; a cascade produces thrombin; thrombin converts fibrin to fibrinogen; fibrinogen then traps erythrocytes.
Platelets stick to each other and to the edges of the cut, forming a solid plug that is itself the clot; no plasma proteins are involved at all.
Blood at the cut is exposed to the air, which converts fibrinogen to fibrin; the fibrin mesh then traps the platelets and erythrocytes to seal the cut.
Platelets release clotting factors; a cascade produces thrombin; thrombin converts fibrinogen to fibrin; fibrin traps erythrocytes.
optionWhy: A student who believes fibrin is the form that circulates picks this reversed sequence. Fibrinogen is the soluble circulating protein; thrombin converts it to insoluble fibrin, which forms the mesh.

A student who has learned only that 'platelets help clotting' picks this. Platelets start the process by releasing clotting factors, but the clot is a mesh of fibrin, made from the plasma protein fibrinogen, trapping erythrocytes.

A student who thinks air triggers clotting picks this. The trigger is the release of clotting factors from platelets at the damaged site; clots form inside the body, with no air present, by the same cascade.

Clotting factors released from platelets start the cascade pathway, which results in rapid conversion of soluble fibrinogen to insoluble fibrin by thrombin. The fibrin mesh traps erythrocytes, forming the clot that seals the cut.
questions.explain: Clotting factors released from platelets start the cascade pathway, which results in rapid conversion of soluble fibrinogen to insoluble fibrin by thrombin. The fibrin mesh traps erythrocytes, forming the clot that seals the cut.

questions.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes the innate immune system from the adaptive immune system?
options: Both systems build up a memory of the pathogens they meet, but the innate system does so faster because it does not need to be specific to each one.
The innate system responds to broad categories of pathogen and does not change during life; the adaptive system is specific and builds a memory of pathogens.
The innate system is the specific one, with each phagocyte recognizing just a single type of pathogen, while the lymphocytes respond to broad categories of pathogen.
The adaptive system responds faster than the innate system on first exposure to a pathogen, because a specific response is a more efficient response.
optionWhy: A student who applies 'building up immunity' to the whole immune system picks this. Only the adaptive system builds a memory; the innate system does not change during an organism's life.

This is the distinction the IB draws. The innate response (including phagocytes) is the same on every exposure, whereas the adaptive response is specific to particular pathogens and becomes more effective because a memory of pathogens encountered is retained.
A student who has attached specificity to the wrong cells picks this. Phagocytes respond to broad categories of pathogen; it is the lymphocytes of the adaptive system that are specific.

A student who assumes the more effective system must be the quicker one picks this. On first exposure the adaptive response takes days, because the few specific lymphocytes must be activated and multiply; the innate response is immediate.
questions.explain: This is the distinction the IB draws. The innate response (including phagocytes) is the same on every exposure, whereas the adaptive response is specific to particular pathogens and becomes more effective because a memory of pathogens encountered is retained.

questions.q: Which statement about B-lymphocytes and antibodies is correct?
options: Each B-lymphocyte examines the antigen it meets and then adjusts the shape of the antibody it makes so that it fits the antigen.
A person has a very large number of different B-lymphocytes, and each of them makes a single specific type of antibody.
Helper T-cells and B-lymphocytes both secrete antibodies, which is why they are said to cooperate in producing them.
B-lymphocytes are found only in the blood; lymph nodes contain trapped pathogens but no lymphocytes at all.
optionWhy: A student who reads 'adaptive' as tailoring picks this. The antibody a B-cell makes is fixed before it meets any antigen; the antigen selects the B-cells that already fit it.

An individual has a very large number of B-lymphocytes that each make a specific type of antibody. The diversity of B-cells, not any tailoring by an individual cell, is what allows a specific response to almost any antigen.
A student who reads 'cooperate' as both making antibody picks this. Only B-lymphocytes produce antibodies; helper T-cells cooperate by activating them.
A student who knows lymphocytes only as white blood cells picks this. Lymphocytes both circulate in the blood and are contained in lymph nodes, which is where many antigens meet them.
questions.explain: An individual has a very large number of B-lymphocytes that each make a specific type of antibody. The diversity of B-cells, not any tailoring by an individual cell, is what allows a specific response to almost any antigen.

questions.q: Which statement about the transmission of HIV is correct?
options: HIV is transmitted in body fluids such as blood, semen, vaginal secretions and breast milk, for example through unprotected sex, shared needles or from mother to child.
HIV is transmitted through the air by coughing, and by casual contact such as shaking hands, sharing cutlery or using the same toilet as an infected person.
HIV is transmitted by blood-feeding insects such as mosquitoes, in the same way as the virus that causes Japanese encephalitis is transmitted.
HIV can only be transmitted by a person who has already developed AIDS, because before that stage the virus is not present in body fluids.
optionWhy: HIV is transmitted in body fluids. The mechanisms include unprotected sexual intercourse, sharing of hypodermic needles, transfusion of unscreened blood or blood products, and transmission from mother to child across the placenta, during birth or in breast milk.

A student who generalizes from colds and contact infections picks this. HIV is not present in sufficient quantity in saliva or on skin, does not survive outside the body and is not transmitted by these routes.
A student who knows HIV is in blood and that mosquitoes carry some viruses picks this. HIV does not replicate in mosquitoes and is not transmitted by insect bites.
A student who treats HIV and AIDS as the same thing picks this. A person with HIV is infectious from soon after infection, often for years before AIDS develops.
questions.explain: HIV is transmitted in body fluids. The mechanisms include unprotected sexual intercourse, sharing of hypodermic needles, transfusion of unscreened blood or blood products, and transmission from mother to child across the placenta, during birth or in breast milk.

questions.q: Why do antibiotics fail to control infections caused by viruses?
options: Viruses are far smaller than bacteria, so antibiotic molecules are too large to bind to them or to enter them effectively.
Antibiotics would destroy the human cells inside which viruses replicate, so they cannot safely be used against a viral infection.
They do not fail: antibiotics kill viruses as well as bacteria, only more slowly, so a longer course is needed for a viral infection.
Viruses have no metabolic processes of their own; they use those of the host cell, which antibiotics do not block.
optionWhy: A student who reaches for size as the explanation picks this. The reason is biochemical: an antibiotic blocks a bacterial process, and a virus has no equivalent process to block, whatever its size.

A student who thinks antibiotics damage human cells picks this. Antibiotics are selective for bacterial processes and do not harm eukaryotic cells; they fail against viruses because there is nothing for them to act on.
A student who sees antibiotics as general anti-infection drugs picks this. Antibiotics have no effect on viruses at any dose or duration, because viruses lack the processes that antibiotics block.

Antibiotics are chemicals that block processes occurring in bacteria but not in eukaryotic cells. A virus has no cell wall, no ribosomes and no metabolism of its own: it reproduces using the eukaryotic host cell's processes, which antibiotics leave untouched.
questions.explain: Antibiotics are chemicals that block processes occurring in bacteria but not in eukaryotic cells. A virus has no cell wall, no ribosomes and no metabolism of its own: it reproduces using the eukaryotic host cell's processes, which antibiotics leave untouched.

questions.q: A hospital ward uses one particular antibiotic heavily. Over several years, an increasing proportion of the bacteria isolated from patients on the ward are found to be resistant to it. Which statement correctly explains this change?
options: Repeated exposure to the antibiotic caused individual bacteria to develop resistance during their own lifetimes, and they passed on this acquired trait to their offspring.
Random mutations had given a few bacteria resistance; the antibiotic killed the susceptible ones, so resistant bacteria survived, reproduced and became more common.
The patients on the ward gradually became resistant to the antibiotic, so it stopped working against the bacteria that were infecting them.
The bacteria became resistant to every antibiotic at the same time, because a single mutation makes a bacterium generally tougher against all drugs.
optionWhy: A student who thinks resistance is a response to exposure picks this. The antibiotic does not cause resistance in an individual bacterium; it selects for bacteria that already carry a resistance mutation.

Resistance evolves by natural selection. Variation from random mutation (or acquired genes) exists before exposure; heavy use of the antibiotic removes the susceptible bacteria and leaves the resistant ones to reproduce, so the resistant proportion rises over time.
A student who locates resistance in the patient picks this. Resistance is a heritable property of the bacterial strain, which is why it is detected in bacteria isolated from patients.

A student who pictures a 'superbug' as generally hardier picks this. Resistance is specific to the process each antibiotic blocks; resistance to several drugs requires several separate genes or mutations.
questions.explain: Resistance evolves by natural selection. Variation from random mutation (or acquired genes) exists before exposure; heavy use of the antibiotic removes the susceptible bacteria and leaves the resistant ones to reproduce, so the resistant proportion rises over time.

questions.q: An mRNA vaccine against COVID-19 contains RNA with the sequence coding for the spike protein of SARS-CoV-2, packaged in lipid nanoparticles. Which statement correctly explains how it stimulates immunity?
options: The RNA is translated into antibodies against the spike protein, which then circulate in the blood ready to bind to the virus.
Cells translate the RNA into spike protein, an antigen that stimulates the adaptive immune system to form memory cells without causing disease.
The RNA produces a weakened form of the whole virus inside the person's cells, giving a mild case of COVID-19 that generates immunity.
The RNA is copied into the DNA of the person's chromosomes, so that their cells will permanently carry and express the gene for the viral antigen.
optionWhy: A student who thinks vaccines supply antibodies picks this. The RNA codes for the antigen, not for antibodies; the person's own B-lymphocytes make the antibodies in response to it.

Vaccines contain antigens, or nucleic acids with sequences that code for antigens, and stimulate the development of immunity to a specific pathogen without causing the disease. The person's cells make the spike protein, and the adaptive response to it leaves memory cells.
A student who thinks a vaccine is a mild dose of the disease picks this. The RNA codes for one protein only; no virus is assembled and the disease does not occur.
A student who blurs RNA and DNA picks this. The mRNA is translated in the cytoplasm and then degraded; it does not enter the nucleus or alter the person's genome, and antigen production is temporary.
questions.explain: Vaccines contain antigens, or nucleic acids with sequences that code for antigens, and stimulate the development of immunity to a specific pathogen without causing the disease. The person's cells make the spike protein, and the adaptive response to it leaves memory cells.

questions.q: In a country, the number of new COVID-19 cases recorded per day fell from 2000 in one week to 1600 in the following week. What is the percentage change in the daily number of cases?
options: Fell by 20%
Fell by 25%
Fell by 22%
Fell by 80%
optionWhy: Percentage change = (final − initial) ÷ initial × 100 = (1600 − 2000) ÷ 2000 × 100 = −400 ÷ 2000 × 100 = −20%, a fall of 20%.
A student who divides the change by the final value picks this: 400 ÷ 1600 × 100 = 25%. Percentage change is measured relative to the initial value, 2000.

A student who applies the percentage difference formula picks this: 400 ÷ 1800 × 100 = 22%. Percentage difference uses the mean of the two values and is for comparing two groups; a change over time uses the initial value as the reference.
A student who divides the new value by the old value picks this: 1600 ÷ 2000 × 100 = 80% is the new figure as a percentage of the old one. The change is 80% − 100% = −20%.
questions.explain: Percentage change = (final − initial) ÷ initial × 100 = (1600 − 2000) ÷ 2000 × 100 = −400 ÷ 2000 × 100 = −20%, a fall of 20%.
